title: Rust Basics
subtitle: Ownership, borrowing and the most important tools

cards.prompt: How many owners does a value in Rust have at any given time?
cards.note: This is the core rule of ownership. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is freed automatically (drop), without any garbage collector.

cards.prompt: What happens to `a` after `let b = a;` if `a` is a `String`?
cards.note: String does not implement Copy, so ownership moves. Afterwards a is no longer valid. If you need both, write a.clone().

cards.prompt: How many mutable references (`&mut`) to a value may exist at the same time?
cards.note: Either any number of &T or exactly one &mut T, never both at once. This is how the compiler rules out data races at compile time.

cards.prompt: What does `'a` stand for in `fn f<'a>(x: &'a str) -> &'a str`?
cards.note: Lifetimes don't extend anything; they only describe relationships: the returned reference lives at most as long as x. Often you can leave them out (lifetime elision).

cards.prompt: Which type expresses that a value may be missing?
cards.note: Option<T> is either Some(value) or None. Rust has no null: if you work with a value that might be missing, you have to handle the None case explicitly.

cards.prompt: What are the two variants of `Result<T, E>`?
cards.note: Ok(T) holds the success value, Err(E) the error. Result is marked #[must_use]: if you ignore it, the compiler warns you.

cards.prompt: What does the `?` operator do when it hits an `Err`?
cards.note: ? exits the function early and passes the error up, converting it through the From trait first. On Ok it simply unwraps the value. It works the same way with Option.

cards.prompt: What happens when you call `.unwrap()` on a `None`?
cards.note: unwrap is handy for prototypes and tests. In real code, ?, match, if let or unwrap_or are usually better. expect with a message at least gives you a clear error message.

cards.prompt: How do you describe behavior shared by several types in Rust?
cards.note: A trait defines methods that types implement: impl Trait for Type. There is no class inheritance; behavior is shared through traits and composition.

cards.prompt: What does the compiler require of every `match`?
cards.note: Every possible value must be covered, if necessary with the wildcard _. If a new enum variant is added later, the compiler points you to every place you need to update.

cards.prompt: Which smart pointer puts a value on the heap, with exactly one owner?
cards.note: You need Box, for example, for recursive types like trees or for trait objects like Box<dyn Error>. The pointer itself has a fixed size; the contents live on the heap.

cards.prompt: Which type allows multiple owners, but only within a single thread?
cards.note: Rc counts references (reference counting). The counter is not atomic and therefore fast, but Rc is not Send. Rc::clone creates another owner, not a deep copy.

cards.prompt: Which type shares ownership safely across multiple threads?
cards.note: Arc stands for Atomically Reference Counted. On its own it only allows shared reading. To modify the value, you usually combine it with Mutex or RwLock: Arc<Mutex<T>>.

cards.prompt: Which command creates a new Rust project in a new folder?
cards.note: cargo new creates the folder with Cargo.toml, src/main.rs and a Git repository. For a folder that already exists, there is cargo init.

cards.prompt: Which command finds common mistakes and unidiomatic code?
cards.note: Clippy knows hundreds of lints. cargo fmt only formats, and cargo check only verifies that the code compiles, without building a binary.

cards.prompt: What does it mean if a type is `Send`?
cards.note: Send is a marker trait without methods that the compiler implements automatically. Rc<T>, for example, is not Send, because otherwise two threads could update its counter at the same time.

cards.prompt: A type `T` is `Sync` if ...?
cards.note: Sync means that several threads may access the value through &T at the same time. Cell and RefCell are not Sync, whereas Mutex<T> is, as long as T is Send.

cards.prompt: Iterators are lazy. Which method collects the elements into a `Vec`, for example?
cards.note: map or filter do nothing on their own. Only a consuming call like collect, sum or a for loop drives the iterator. You specify the target type with an annotation or the turbofish: collect::<Vec<_>>().

cards.prompt: Which method consumes a `Vec` and yields the elements themselves instead of references?
cards.note: iter() yields &T, iter_mut() yields &mut T, and into_iter() yields T and takes ownership of the Vec. A for loop over v calls into_iter, while a loop over &v calls iter.

cards.prompt: How do you recognize a macro call like `println!`?
cards.note: Macros are expanded into code at compile time. That is why println! can take a variable number of arguments and check the format string while compiling.

cards.prompt: What is the type of `&v[1..3]` if `v` is a `Vec<i32>`?
cards.note: A slice is a view into a contiguous range, without copying. Internally, &[T] is a fat pointer made of an address and a length. The range 1..3 covers indices 1 and 2.

cards.prompt: Which string type owns its data and can grow?
cards.note: String lives on the heap and belongs to you; &str is just a borrowed view of UTF-8 text. As a function parameter, &str is usually more flexible, because &String converts to it automatically.

cards.prompt: What is the type of the literal `"hello"`?
cards.note: String literals are baked into the binary and therefore live for the entire program. With .to_string() or String::from you turn one into an owned String.

cards.prompt: What happens with `let x = 5; let x = x + 1;`?
cards.answer: A new x shadows the old one
cards.note: This is called shadowing. The second let creates a new variable, which may even have a different type, as in let input = input.trim(); Both x stay immutable.

cards.prompt: What do you need to be able to reassign `x` later?
cards.note: Variables in Rust are immutable by default. mut is a deliberate choice that shows at a glance where something can change.
